text:
Was stoked to see the post. Went to do evals against the other browser fetch tools that my personal AI harness uses. Expand used fewer tokens but the accuracy was abysmal. 

Details written by Claude:

Benchmark: 6 ways for an AI agent to read a website. curl, agent-browser, Playwright MCP, WebFetch, and two modes of https://t.co/cRr04iCtN9. 270 runs, one answering model (Haiku 5.5), 15 questions.

Setup: one public event site (~50 pages). 15 factual questions in 5 tiers: single page, multi-hop, synthesis, conflicting or unpublished facts, JS-rendered. 3 repeats each. A blind Sonnet 5.5 judge graded against known answers.

Accuracy:
curl 82%
agent-browser 78%
Playwright 69%
WebFetch 64%
https://t.co/cRr04iCtN9 Fetch 53%
https://t.co/cRr04iCtN9 Highlights 31%

The top four have overlapping 95% intervals, so no ranking among them is supported. The bottom two are clearly behind.

Cost differs a lot. Median tokens per question: WebFetch ~15k, agent-browser ~80k, curl ~160k. curl wins by reading more pages (median 13 tool calls). WebFetch is cheapest, but it read a stale banner on the JS countdown: 17% on that tier vs 83% for curl and the browsers.

Hardest tier: two pages disagreed ("mandatory" vs "strongly recommended"). curl caught the conflict 78% of the time. agent-browser 33%, Playwright 11%. Both read one page and answered with confidence.

https://t.co/cRr04iCtN9: its own benchmark says it beats other fetchers. Not seen here. On this easy site it used ~4x WebFetch's tokens and scored lower. Highlights reads one page per call, so multi-page questions often failed. The test site is easier than theirs, so this is no verdict on their benchmark.

Limits: one site, 15 questions, a small answering model. 78 of 270 grades were hand-checked. Fixing a vague question and a too-lenient rubric moved numbers a few points, not the order.

text:
This looks like a big step for agents that read the web.

Expand, a new AI startup, released Expand Fetch, a tool that lets AI agents read web pages without losing icons, tables and hidden data along the way. 
On Expand’s own private test, agents using it answered 74% of hard web questions correctly, against 55% for the next best tool.

When AI agents read a website today, the page is usually converted to plain text first, and details like a ✗ next to a feature get thrown away, so the agent confidently gives wrong answers. 

Expand Fetch, uses its own vision model, Iris, to look at the page the way a person does and keep those details intact.

Every fetch is also stored as a snapshot whose Markdown lines link back to their source, letting developers trace a wrong answer to what the agent saw.

text:
The checkmarks on a pricing page have no words in them. That one dumb fact is why your AI keeps getting basic questions wrong.

Ask an AI which plan comes with a feature, which flight includes a bag, which apartment allows dogs. It answers fast and sounds sure. But most AI tools never look at the page. They run it through a converter that strips everything down to text, and a ✓ or ✗ in a comparison table is an icon, so it just disappears. The cell comes back empty. The model fills in the blank and tells you the Business plan has an uptime SLA when it never did.

I only clocked how bad this is when I saw the numbers. One benchmark ran the same model, Claude Sonnet 5.5, over the same 326 hard web pages through three different scraping APIs. Accuracy went 27%, 55%, 74%. Nothing about the model changed. The only thing that changed was how much of the page it got to see.

Converters like that were built around 2010 for a human reading an article on their phone. Strip the nav, find the paragraphs, done. Agents want the opposite stuff: the table, the badge, the price toggle, and all the data a page quietly loads as JSON in the background (store locations, inventory counts, the customer logos). Text scrapers never touch that layer, and it’s usually the whole reason the agent went there.

Expand’s answer is almost childishly simple: look at the page. A vision model reads the rendered screenshot the way you would, tables and icons intact, and a second model pulls the hidden JSON out from underneath. Tim was a founding engineer at Prisma, so this is his second run at the boring layer between a developer and their data. The 74% comes from a benchmark his team built with customers, so hold it loosely, but a 47-point spread is hard to argue with.

We have spent three years ranking models. For agents, a 20-point gap between scrapers is now bigger than the gap between the top models on the same task. The next big jump in AI reliability will come from what the model gets to see, and nobody will credit the model for it.

Another great application of System One models. 

I think much of what we call hallucination in web agents comes from misreading the page. 

When a page is flattened to text, a small ✗ in a pricing table disappears, and the agent answers incorrectly with full confidence. 

Expand Fetch reads the rendered page, returns the underlying data as clean JSON, and keeps a replay of exactly what your agent saw.
